strengths: Clear and well-motivated framework (SGShift) for diagnosing and explaining concept shift, which is a critical and under-explored area compared to covariate shift.
Novel integration of sparse Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) with model misspecification absorption and Model-X knockoffs for rigorous false discovery control.
Solid theoretical backing, including a convergence guarantee under Restricted Strong Convexity (RSC) and formal FDR/PFER control bounds under stability selection.
Extensive empirical evaluation across multiple semi-synthetic and real-world clinical datasets, demonstrating substantial improvements in AUC and Recall compared to existing baselines.
The manuscript is exceptionally well-written, structured, and easy to follow, with code provided for reproducibility.
weaknesses: Lack of detail regarding the choice and construction of basis functions in the main text. It is unclear what specific basis functions are used (e.g., splines, linear, or polynomial) and how this choice scales or impacts performance.

Limited discussion on computational complexity. Running stability selection with Model-X knockoffs (requiring B iterations of optimization) can be computationally expensive on large tabular datasets, and some discussion or reporting of wall-clock times would be beneficial.

The theoretical guarantees rely on standard assumptions like sub-Gaussian features and independence for knockoffs. Since clinical tabular data often exhibits highly non-linear dependencies and extreme collinearity, a discussion of the empirical robustness of the FDR control when these assumptions are violated would strengthen the work.

strengths: The paper addresses a highly important and practical problem: identifying and attributing concept shift (changes in p(y|X)) to specific features in tabular datasets.
The proposed method, SGShift, is conceptually elegant, leveraging Sparse Generalized Additive Models (GAMs) to construct interpretable updates.
The inclusion of the absorption term (SGShift-A) to handle model misspecification and knockoffs (SGShift-K) for false discovery rate control shows excellent methodological depth.
The paper provides rigorous theoretical guarantees, including convergence bounds under Restricted Strong Convexity (RSC) and FDR/PFER control for the stability selection knockoffs.

Extensive semi-synthetic and real-world experiments on healthcare datasets (Diabetes Readmission, COVID-19, SUPPORT2) demonstrate that SGShift significantly and consistently outperforms existing baselines.
weaknesses: The choice of the basis functions φ(X) is not clearly explained in the main text. It is important to clarify whether these are linear terms, splines, or other transformations, as the complexity and interpretability of the GAM term highly depend on this choice.

The performance of SGShift under dense (non-sparse) concept shifts is not thoroughly analyzed. While the paper acknowledges this limitation in the discussion, some empirical or theoretical exploration of how the model degrades under dense shift would be valuable.

Comparison with baselines is somewhat narrow, though understandable given the lack of direct competitors. Exploring or discussing connections with causal discovery or invariant learning methods that also aim to pinpoint shifted mechanisms could strengthen the related work and evaluation.

strengths: Addresses an important and highly practical problem: explaining concept shift ($p(y|X)$ changes) in tabular data by identifying a sparse set of shifted features.
The proposed model (SGShift) is elegant, modeling the shift as a sparse additive update (GAM) on top of an existing black-box source model.
The incorporation of Model-X knockoffs with stability selection provides rigorous statistical guarantees (FDR and PFER control) for feature selection under distribution shift.
The addition of an absorption term via a difference-in-difference formulation is a clever and effective way to decouple actual concept shift from source model misspecification.
Extensive empirical evaluations across several medical datasets demonstrate significant improvements in AUC and recall compared to existing methods like WhyShift and SHAP.
weaknesses: The theoretical assumption in Theorem 4.1 and Lemma .1 that the loss Hessian is uniformly bounded away from zero ($\nabla^2 \ell \ge \kappa > 0$) is violated for logistic regression (the loss used in the Diabetes and COVID-19 datasets) because the Hessian approaches zero as the predictions become extreme. This requires restricting the predictors/parameters to a compact domain, which should be explicitly stated and discussed.

Constructing valid Model-X knockoffs for tabular datasets containing mixed data types (e.g., continuous variables alongside categorical features like gender, race, and comorbidity status) is notoriously difficult. If pairwise exchangeability is violated, the FDR/PFER control guarantees in Lemma 4.2 break. The manuscript lacks details on how these knockoffs were practically generated for the complex datasets used in the experiments.

The GAM framework assumes that the concept shift is additive across individual features. If the shift involves complex, high-order feature interactions, this additive assumption may fail to correctly capture or attribute the shift.
The paper does not detail how the hierarchical regularization parameters ($\lambda_\omega$ and $\lambda_\delta$) in the absorption models are chosen or tuned in practice.

Minor presentation issues and typos are present, such as 'Regardless the amount of data' (should be 'Regardless of the...') on page 1, 'koint distribution' (should be 'joint distribution') in Appendix A.3, and referring to Figure 1 on page 7 before it actually appears on page 8.

strengths: Strongly motivated and clearly written manuscript tackling the challenging and practically important problem of diagnosing concept shift.

The proposed method, SGShift, is highly principled: framing concept shift explanation as learning a sparse correction term while treating the source model as an offset is elegant and computationally lightweight.

The inclusion of advanced variants—specifically SGShift-A to absorb source model misspecification and SGShift-K utilizing Model-X knockoffs for formal false-discovery/PFER control—greatly enhances the method's practical utility and reliability.

Solid theoretical guarantees are provided, demonstrating estimation consistency under standard high-dimensional assumptions (cone-restricted strong convexity) without requiring parametric assumptions on the underlying regression function.

Extensive and rigorous experimental evaluation across multiple tabular datasets (e.g., healthcare, genomics) showing significant performance improvements over existing baselines across diverse settings (varying sample sizes, model mismatches, correlation levels, and high-dimensionality).
Compelling real-world case studies with biological and clinical verification (such as COVID-19 variant severity shifts and ancestry-associated genetic markers for Lupus).
weaknesses: The paper could benefit from a clearer discussion on how covariate shift interacts with the identification of concept shift. If the target distribution $P_T(X)$ has very low or zero support in regions where the concept shift occurs, the target design might fail to satisfy the restricted strong convexity (RSC) condition, limiting the method's ability to identify those shifted features.

The baselines could be more exhaustive. For example, a straightforward baseline of training sparse models (like Lasso) independently on both source and target domains and comparing their coefficient supports ('Lasso-diff') would help isolate the specific benefits of using the source model as a fixed offset.

The linear/generalized additive formulation for the correction term $\phi(X)^\top \delta$ assumes that the shift can be well-represented by a sparse linear combination of basis functions. If the true concept shift is highly non-linear and not easily captured by the chosen basis $\phi$, the feature selection quality might degrade, which is not thoroughly discussed.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and challenging problem in distribution shift: identifying which sparse set of features is responsible for concept shift (changes in the conditional distribution P(Y|X)).

The proposed formulation (using the source model as a fixed offset and learning a sparse correction term) is simple, elegant, and theoretically sound, enabling the use of established high-dimensional statistics tools.

The paper provides rigorous theoretical guarantees, including estimation consistency under restricted strong convexity (Theorem 3.1 & 3.2) and false-discovery rate control via Model-X knockoffs (Theorem 3.3).

The empirical evaluation is highly comprehensive, spanning multiple semi-synthetic configurations, dense and sparse settings, varying sample sizes, high-dimensional setups, and different machine learning model architectures.

The real-world case studies in healthcare (COVID-19 pre/post Omicron) and genomics (Lupus ancestry differences) provide practical validation, showing that the identified features match known domain literature.
weaknesses: The assumption of a linear correction term on the link scale (Equation 1) might be restrictive if the concept shift is highly non-linear or involves complex multi-way interactions. Although Appendix K explores pairwise interactions, the scalability and performance of the method with arbitrary non-linear basis expansions remain a limitation.

The computational scalability of the knockoff-based variant (SGShift-K) is not discussed. Generating high-quality Model-X knockoffs for complex tabular distributions and running repeated optimization paths can be computationally expensive as the number of features p and sample size n increase.

The method's performance still depends on the quality of the source model h_S. Although the absorption term in SGShift-A mitigates misspecification, a more systematic stress-test showing how the accuracy of feature selection degrades with increasingly worse source models would strengthen the work.
Some of the figures (e.g., Figure 1 and Figure 4 in the appendix) have very small text and tightly crowded legends, which can make visual comparison difficult for the reader.

strengths: Elegant formulation: Framing the identification of concept-shifted features as learning a sparse correction term over a fixed source-model offset is highly intuitive, mathematically clean, and directly avoids the error accumulation issues inherent in separate-model 'plugin' approaches.
Solid theoretical guarantees: The paper provides rigorous consistency bounds under local restricted strong convexity (RSC) and formal error control (PFER and FDR) using derandomized knockoffs.

Thorough evaluation: The benchmarking is extensive, covering mismatched base/generator models, dense vs. sparse shifts, varying target sample sizes, high dimensionality, collinearity, and low signal-to-noise ratios. It significantly outperforms competitive baselines.

Clinically and biologically plausible case studies: The real-world experiments on COVID-19 hospitalization (Omicron variant shift) and Lupus genetic markers successfully recover meaningful and documented features, validating the practical utility of the tool.
weaknesses: Sparsity assumption: The method's theoretical foundations and motivation rely on a sparse correction. Although empirical results on dense simulations are strong, a deeper conceptual discussion of why L1 regularization behaves so robustly as a ranking heuristic under dense shifts would strengthen the paper.

Dependency on the basis map: The success of the feature selection depends on the choice of the basis map $\phi(X)$. If the true distribution shift is highly non-linear or involves complex multi-way interactions, standard linear/pairwise bases might fail to capture the shift unless the feature space is significantly over-specified, potentially introducing high-dimensional estimation challenges.

Knockoff dependence on $P(X)$: SGShift-K relies on generating valid Model-X knockoffs, which requires accurate estimation of the covariate distribution. In scenarios where covariate shift also occurs alongside concept shift, estimating the target-domain feature distribution reliably can be difficult, potentially degrading the FDR control in practice.
